title: A Causality-Gated Multi-Agent System for Generative Feature Engineering in Financial Markets
abstract: Systems that ask a large language model to emit executable feature code inherit a failure surface that hand-curated feature engineering does not have: the generated code can reference future information in ways no syntactic scan can see. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a behavioral admission test for machine-generated code; the engineering application is the automated construction and validation of predictive features for financial time-series forecasting. We present a provider-agnostic multi-agent system in which an eight-node LangGraph orchestration is fronted by a behavioral causality gate that admits a candidate only if perturbing the raw input of a single day leaves every earlier output day unchanged, deciding admissibility from what the code computes, not how it is written. The gate needs no model call, costs nine feature recomputations per candidate, and rejects 93.8% of confirmed leakers at a 0.04% false-rejection rate. We validate the system on daily open-to-close direction for S&P 100 equities, with four large-language-model configurations mounted in turn as its generator. Probing all 4,559 candidates confirms 81 leakers that a conventional negative-shift guard had admitted, including the nominal best feature at 68.3% accuracy, and removing them overturns the naive model ranking. Causal hygiene is strongly capability-dependent: 11.8% of the weakest generator's pool leaks against none of 3,373 candidates from the two strongest, making the choice of generator a safety decision as well as a quality one. Under nested validation the accuracy advantage is largely within noise, locating the system's value in tail-discovery rather than in a uniform gain.
why: Real LLM failure mode, behavioral causality gate, implementable this quarter.

title: Adaptive Domain-Aware Semantic Caching for Vietnamese Banking RAG Assistants under Time-Varying Workloads
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in banking face two compounding bottlenecks: the high per-query cost of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the bursty, time-varying nature of customer traffic. General-purpose semantic caches apply a single similarity threshold and a fixed eviction policy to all queries, which is inadequate for a domain where reusing a stale interest-rate answer carries far greater risk than reusing one about branch hours. In a preliminary study, we introduced a domain-aware cache with hand-set per-intent thresholds and time-to-live values. This paper extends that work along four axes. First, we replace the handset thresholds with a Bayesian Threshold Adapter (BTA) that learns per-intent similarity thresholds from quality feedback; the compliance safety floor demonstrably binds as a brake—two financially sensitive intents relax exactly to their 0.90 floor and no further. Second, we derive per-intent TTL values from observed answer volatility. Third, we contribute an Apache Kafka streaming architecture as a deployment blueprint (its empirical evaluation is future work). Fourth, we evaluate under a time-varying protocol that injects all 248 scheduled gold-answer updates over eight simulated banking days on a newly crawled, human-reviewed corpus of 481 Vietnamese FAQ pairs from three major banks (a 2{,}405-query replay with full provenance). Measured on a single consumer GPU, the proposed system raises throughput from 0.41 to 8.15 queries per second (20.1$\times$; 94.5\% LLM-call reduction), cuts P95 latency from 6,666ms to 447ms, and roughly halves the rate at which financially sensitive queries are answered with the wrong FAQ item relative to a global-threshold cache, at a cost of 2.3 raw hit-rate points. The entire system runs on free, lightweight open models.
why: Real banking RAG system; missing results and evidence.

title: Geopolitical Oil Supply Shocks, Household Loss Aversion, and Macro-Financial Spill over from the US-Israel-Iran Conflict
abstract: We analyze the transmission of conflict-driven energy-security shocks in a monthly structural VAR linking oil prices, AI/LLM oil-related geopolitical risk, U.S. macro-financial conditions, household fundamentals, and emerging-market asset prices. The estimated responses trace uncertainty and financial conditions, energy-price pass-through, international asset-market spillovers, and household income and consumption. Oil-price-shock responses show delayed food-and-gas price pressure alongside weaker consumption and industrial production, indicating a stagflationary risk in the shock response. We supplement the VAR with local projections of the range-based method-of-moments local mimicking loss aversion (MMLA) index for household income and consumption. The controlled consumption MMLA index rises at 24 months; the oil-episode coefficient for the income MMLA outcome is negative and only marginally significant. Forecast-error decompositions distinguish the persistent own-shock component of oil-related geopolitical risk from the oil-price innovation under alternative recursive orderings. In a separate synthetic three-lag scenario, oil and geopolitical risk decline by May 2028 while consumption weakens and VIX rises; the negative policy-rate point forecast has a wide band that also includes positive rates. The scenario is not itself a stagflation point forecast or an identified Federal Reserve reaction. The results suggest that energy-security events can transmit through several international macro-financial channels rather than oil prices alone.
why: Traditional macro VAR; LLM framing in abstract, contribution elsewhere.

title: Evolution of Artificial Intelligence in Banking: Evidence from Bibliometric Analysis of Collaborative Networks and Research Trends
abstract: In this study, we examine the research trends and collaboration networks in AI-driven transformation in banking by utilizing 751 Scopus-indexed documents from 2020 to 2026. We found that the number of publications continues to grow until 2024, and the literature is spread out over a series of conference proceedings, with a core set of highly cited foundational papers that define the overall landscape of research. In addition, keyword analysis and mapping of conceptual structure indicate a core set of research focused on applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning to risk management, fraud detection, cybersecurity, and market analysis. Thematic mapping of the search results shows that "artificial intelligence in banking" is a core theme, while generative AI, including ChatGPT and large language models, is a niche theme. The motor themes quadrant shows a sparse set of papers, which indicates that cutting-edge areas are still in their infancy. Further, we found that national production is dominated by a single predominant producer, while fragmented co-authorship networks are evident, with a mere 23.7% international collaboration. The study further proposes a future research agenda that includes the integration of GenAI with fundamental banking tasks, adversarial robustness, explainability and fairness, and impact, with the aim of shifting from a niche theme to a field-defining motor theme. This broadening area of artificial intelligence in banking also accelerates SDG 8(Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 9(Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure).
why: Bibliometric survey; explicitly rejected by stated preferences.

title: The Greening Effect of Green Bonds on Corporate Energy Transition: Micro Evidence from Chinese A-Listed Firms aLI Bohua1, aSUI Yuan2, aJIA Kaiwei3, aWU Jinjin4
abstract: Amidst deepening global climate governance, whether green bonds genuinely drive corporate energy restructuring remains contested. This study examines the causal effect of green bond issuance on corporate energy structure transition using a unique micro-dataset of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2013 to 2024. Grounded in a Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) production function framework, we model green bonds as a mechanism that reduces the user cost of clean energy capital, thereby altering firms' optimal fossil-to-clean energy substitution path. To establish causality, we employ two-way fixed effects and an ensemble Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) estimator, which flexibly captures treatment effect heterogeneity while addressing high-dimensional confounding. Empirical results reveal three novel findings: First, green bond issuance induces a significantly positive and scale-increasing substitution effect​ toward cleaner energy. Second, green technology innovation​ mediates this transition, with incremental innovation​ demonstrating a stronger transmission channel than radical innovation—suggesting that green finance primarily facilitates gradual optimization rather than disruptive technological leaps. Third, and counter-intuitively, financing constraints positively moderate​ the greening effect, whereas high ESG ratings exhibit negative moderation, revealing a "diminishing marginal return" pattern for sustainability incumbents. These findings provide micro-empirical evidence for calibrating green finance policies and highlight that green bonds are most potent for firms facing urgent transition pressures.
why: Single-country policy study; ML is tool, not contribution.

title: The unintended distributional consequences of public data openness: Evidence from regional debt financing dispersion in China
abstract: Abstract: This study examines the distributional consequences of public data openness for regional debt financing. Exploiting the staggered rollout of municipal public data platforms across Chinese cities from 2009 to 2023, we find that public data openness significantly increases within-city debt financing dispersion. The financing gains accrue disproportionately to state-owned enterprises, more digitalized firms, and firms with stronger government–business connections. This effect is amplified by local artificial intelligence development but mitigated by a better information environment, stronger financial regulation, and higher local governance efficiency. These findings demonstrate that public data openness can widen financing disparities despite reducing information frictions, highlighting the importance of institutional safeguards in promoting more inclusive use of public data and data-driven technologies.
why: Data-policy effects in China; not ML methods work.

title: From Agent-Based Models to LLM-Based Financial Agents: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review, Multidimensional Taxonomy, and Future Research Agenda
abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used in finance to model market interactions, optimize sequential decisions, and coordinate specialized analytical tasks. However, the field remains fragmented across agent-based modeling, multi-agent reinforcement learning, LLM-based multi-agent systems, and hybrid architectures. This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic review of financial multi-agent systems. Searches in Scopus and Web of Science identified 906 records. After screening, full-text assessment, and a post-extraction scope audit, 93 primary studies were retained for quantitative and thematic synthesis, while seven secondary publications were analyzed separately for contextual positioning. The results show that the literature is dominated by MARL and LLM-based multi-agent systems, followed by ABM and hybrid approaches. Portfolio management, algorithmic trading, and market simulation are the main application domains. Real financial data remain dominant, whereas textual and multimodal data are increasingly used in LLM-based systems. Evaluation is largely based on backtesting, predictive accuracy, and financial performance, with limited attention to robustness, explainability, reproducibility, human validation, regulatory alignment, and real-world deployment. The paper proposes a multidimensional taxonomy and a research agenda for transparent, robust, risk-aware, and trustworthy financial multi-agent systems.
why: Systematic review; explicitly rejected survey category.
